perspective:
As Carolyn Abebe, my available information is:

- I am a bank teller at a community bank. Marilyn Olson is a colleague/sales representative there; we recently began working together.
- During a busy week at the bank, I noticed Marilyn was unusually quiet and withdrawn, unlike her normally engaging demeanor.
- I asked Marilyn if she was alright and if she wanted to talk. She told me she was a bit overwhelmed with work and some personal stuff, and thanked me for asking.
- In a later interaction, Marilyn was curt with me. I felt confused and slightly hurt. I told her I hoped I hadn’t overstepped, that I’d had tough times too, and that talking can sometimes help. She said she appreciated that, apologized if she seemed off, and said it had been a hard week.
- Marilyn appeared to respond positively to my openness. I felt relieved and hopeful. I invited her to a small get-together with friends that weekend. She said it sounded lovely, thanked me, and said she would love to join.
- Despite friendly interactions outside work, I felt Marilyn was still maintaining a professional distance at the bank. I felt disappointed and asked to talk about our work dynamic and the distance I couldn’t understand. She said she hadn’t realized it, apologized if it seemed that way, and agreed to talk about improving collaboration.
- After our private meeting, I believed we had cleared the air and better understood each other’s professional expectations and personal boundaries. I felt content and optimistic. I proposed teaming up on the new project proposal. Marilyn said it was a great idea, was glad we had the talk, and looked forward to working more closely with me.
- I do not have access to Marilyn’s private thoughts, hidden events, or anything she did not tell me or show through her behavior in these interactions.
